ablaut.html: writ(e) + t + en → written The e of -en is said, and on its own it would reach back and make the i long: writen would read “wright-en.” The doubled t is a block box: the vault stops there, and the i stays short.
When the past is spelled o-consonant-e, the -en form keeps the o and its vault: spoke, spoken ; broke, broken ; stole, stolen ; woke, woken ; wove, woven ; froze, frozen ; chose, chosen .
There the -en form goes back to an i, and the i is short, behind a box where the consonant can double and without one where it can’t or doesn’t.

The o is the verb's ending for I, in Greek and Latin alike (leg-o, gather-I), so it is a morpheme of its own; read instead as the linking o of biology, it still sits between seams.

a seam before the e, which keeps the vault back to the o The e of -ed takes over the silent e's job, as the i does in hoping.
box on ll, a seam between the two l's, a blocked vault from the y The two l's come from two parts but spell one sound, as the ee of been does.
the e after the seam in a cone, with a vault back to the i The e of like and the e of -ed are one e.

notate + ion: ti as a green unit across a seam, the t black and the i red, with the vault sent from the i Ruled 8 November 2026: the t and i spell sh together, so their bar and circle are green, as for sh, and the letters keep their own colours, so the i is red, and it still makes the a long.
a short o closed by b, and a short i in -in, with no vault As lemon and seven, and as the role cards draw robin.
The i of -in is said lightly but still has the sound of the i in sit, so it takes a short mark, as in music and doing.
a short i closed by v, with no vault, and er as the r-controlled unit As seven and never: a short first vowel takes the consonant into its syllable (riv·er), and er is marked as in tiger.
a bare o and an e in a cone, as done Gone has the short o of got for most speakers, and done has the u of up.
two markings each: the verb with a bare first vowel, the noun with a marked one Stress falls on the root in the verb (proDUCE, conDUCT) and on the prefix in the noun (PROduce, CONduct).
Ruled 10 November 2026: the noun produce has a long mark on its o and no vault, since a vault would name a cause the letters don't supply, and capitals show stress in captions.

a long mark on the first vowel and no vault Changed 10 November 2026 at Dante's direction, after the noun produce: these are one part each, and no letter makes the first vowel long, so a vault would name a cause that isn't there.
the e of hope keeps its cone and its vault across the seam; the endings' vowels bare The endings' vowels are said weakly, so they take no mark.
weak vowels bare, ss as a doubled ending, and ble as consonant + le -ful has one l, and the a of -able is bare, as a weak vowel is elsewhere.
ee over every final y 21 November: Keep the ee over a final y that spells ee (happy, city, very), with the box and blocked vault where a double stands before it.
put and do: one oo for two sounds 21 November: ʊ, the International Phonetic Alphabet's letter for the vowel of book, over the u of put and the oo of book; do keeps oo.
elite: ee over a French i 21 November: The final e makes the i long and sends a vault, which lands beside the ee: elite, police, expertise.

ufli.html: For schools that run UFLI Foundations: where its lessons meet the path, the mark to draw alongside each part of UFLI, and why the two orders differ.

UFLI asks that its materials be linked rather than copied (its copyright statement says so), so its lesson names and word lists stay on its own site: its scope and sequence is in the UFLI Foundations Toolbox .
Each band gives what UFLI teaches there, the mark to add, an example or two marked, the steps where the path meets it, and where the two part.
The vowel vault from the e to the vowel it makes long; the nice-nudge to a soft c or g; the cone without a vault in have .
The path teaches one vault for all of them (step 9), and have and give just before it (step 8), so the exception and the rule sit side by side.
tch and dge as the doubled ch and j, in a box after a short vowel; the long mark with no vault ( find ); a red circle under y; one swoop and one circle for le.
A cone only where another form of the word says the letter.
The prepositions ( it, in, on, up ), the pronouns ( I, me, my, he, she, we ) and the pointing words ( this, that, these, those ) are the grammar of every sentence a learner says and reads.
Taught together from the start, they become regular, and the first contrast learners meet is the one the spelling system is built on: I and it , he and hen , no and not .
Split at the meaning, it is act + ion , and the t belongs to the base, which is why it keeps turning up in actor and active .
The path puts the vault, the box and the dropped e at steps 9, 14 and 15, so hoping and hopping are one system: the box blocks the vault, and the dropped e lets it through.

Most heart words are regular once their step comes on the path ( could , both , learn ), or have a reason a learner can use ( said from say ; the o of son , month and love ); only a few are left to learn by heart.
Both orders are systematic, and research doesn’t favour one systematic order over another: the National Reading Panel’s 38 phonics studies used about 19 different sequences, and they all worked.
What can be counted is which of the words learners meet most each order lets them decode, and when: the 148 high-frequency words of the Early Literacy Profile (Central Okanagan) and Dolch’s 220.
On Dolch’s lists the two are even at that point: his first lists have many closed words ( big, can, red, run ) that UFLI’s letter-by-letter order reaches as fast.
By the time it finishes the first r-controlled units, UFLI has also taught open syllables in longer words, endings, consonant + le and long vowels before two consonants.

The path teaches those after its r-controlled step (steps 13 to 18), so at that point UFLI reads 26 ELP words the path doesn’t yet, among them come , some , small , little , write , over , before , under , both , old .

The difference is no longer order: it is the words the path teaches with a reason and UFLI teaches as heart words: the , to , you , said , two , into , who , again , any , could , would , from , walk , does , many , their , your , together , other .
A word counts on the path from the step whose list has it, or from the latest step among the things it needs (its letters, units and marks), whichever is earlier.
In UFLI it counts from the first lesson whose Roll and Read page uses it (UFLI leaves heart words off those pages), or from the latest lesson among the things it needs, whichever is earlier.
On 1,907 words of five letters or fewer from the Roll and Read pages, placing by what a word needs gave the lesson UFLI first uses it in 88% of words, and within three lessons in 91%.
Dots on the dashed line come in the same order in both programs; dots above it, the path gets to sooner, and dots below it, UFLI does.
The nasal sound is said, not spelled.

word-lists.html: Apart from and , is and it in kindergarten, the ELP’s only short-vowel words are on its Digraphs list, so it seems to leave the rest to phonics lessons.

The silent e list pulls five , gave , made , these , those , use and write into grade 1 from Dolch’s second grade, while the diphthong list holds 10 early words such as how , round and down back to grade 2.
